lead: An isolated footing is a slab under a single column. It spreads the column load over enough soil to keep the pressure safe, and it bends upward like an upside-down cantilever slab on every side of the column. Its plan comes from the soil; its depth usually comes from shear, either one-way shear across the width or punching shear round the column; and its steel comes from bending at the column face. Square and rectangular pads are the commonest; a column moment makes the pressure uneven, and a sloped top saves concrete in large pads. Every framed building in India stands on footings like these.
prereq: You need the wall-footing steps of Wall footings, and the shear strength τc and development length Ld (see Design of shear reinforcement and Bond, anchorage and development length).

blocks.text: Size the plan with service loads: A = (P + Wf)/qs, where P is the column load, Wf the footing weight (start with 10 % of P) and qs the safe bearing capacity. A square pad has side √A; a circular pad has diameter √(4A/π). For a rectangular column, make the projections equal on all sides (L − a = B − b, where a × b is the column), so that both directions carry similar moments.

With a column moment M (service), the pressure varies across the length: p = (P + W<sub>f</sub>)/A ± M/Z, with Z = BL²/6 for bending along L. Keep p<sub>max</sub> ≤ q<sub>s</sub> and p<sub>min</sub> ≥ 0, which means e = M/P ≤ L/6. An alternative is to shift the footing by e so its centroid sits under the resultant, which makes the pressure uniform again for that load case.

sections.h3: Design for bending, shear and anchorage

blocks.text: Use the net factored pressure wu = Pu/A (or the trapezoid from Pu and Mu); the footing weight is left out. IS 456 clause 34 then fixes four checks:

items: Bending at the column face, in each direction, on the full width: Mu = wuB × (projection)²/2.
One-way shear at distance d from the column face, across the full width: τv = Vu/(Bd) ≤ τc (Table 19, with the pt provided).
Punching shear on a perimeter d/2 from the column faces: Vu = Pu − wu(a + d)(b + d), b0 = 2(a + b + 2d), τv = Vu/(b0d) ≤ ks × 0.25√fck, with ks = 0.5 + b/a ≤ 1.
Anchorage: bars extend Ld beyond the column face; column bars extend Ld (in compression) into the footing; bearing under the column is limited to 0.45fck√(A1/A2) with √(A1/A2) ≤ 2.

blocks.text: In a rectangular pad the long bars are spread evenly across B. The short bars are not: IS 456 clause 34.3.1(b) puts 2/(β + 1) of them in a central band of width B, where β = L/B, and the rest evenly in the two end strips. Minimum steel is 0.12 % of the gross section in each direction for Fe415.

A large pad can be thick at the column and taper to an edge of at least 150 mm (IS 456 clause 34.1.2). The slope is kept gentle enough to cast without a top shutter, and a flat ledge of about 75 mm is left round the column for its formwork. Every check is then made with the depth at its own section: bending at the column face uses the full depth there, but only the concrete above the neutral axis counts in compression, so the narrow flat top limits the compression width; one-way shear at d from the face uses the reduced depth and the trapezoidal section at that line; punching uses the depth at d/2 from the face.

examples.question: A 300 mm × 500 mm column carries a service load of 1200 kN. The safe bearing capacity is 200 kN/m². Design a rectangular footing with M20 concrete and Fe415 bars.
steps: Plan: A = 1.1 × 1200/200 = 6.60 m². Equal projections need L − B = 0.5 − 0.3 = 0.2 m, so B(B + 0.2) = 6.60, B = 2.47 m. Adopt L × B = 2.7 m × 2.5 m = 6.75 m²; both projections are (2.7 − 0.5)/2 = (2.5 − 0.3)/2 = 1.10 m.

Moment per metre at either face: 266.67 × 1.10²/2 = 161.33 kN·m/m; d for bending = √(161.33 × 10⁶/2760) = 242 mm. Punching alone would need d ≈ 440 mm; one-way shear needs more. Adopt D = 600 mm, d = 600 − 50 − 16 = 534 mm (average of the two layers).

One-way shear at d from the long face: V<sub>u</sub> = 266.67 × 2.5 × (1.10 − 0.534) = 377.3 kN, τ<sub>v</sub> = 377333/(2500 × 534) = 0.283 N/mm². With 11 bars of 16 mm, p<sub>t</sub> = 0.166 % and τ<sub>c</sub> = 0.293 N/mm² ≥ τ<sub>v</sub>. The other direction gives the same stress.

Steel along L (moment 403.3 kN·m on 2.5 m): A<sub>st</sub> = 2165 mm² (minimum 1800); 11 bars of 16 mm = 2212 mm². Steel along B (moment 435.6 kN·m on 2.7 m): 2338 mm² (minimum 1944); 12 bars of 16 mm = 2413 mm².
Central band: β = 2.7/2.5 = 1.08, 2/(β + 1) = 0.962, so 11.5 → 12 of the 12 short bars go in the central 2.5 m band; with β this close to 1 the spacing is almost uniform.
Anchorage: L<sub>d</sub> of a 16 mm bar = 47 × 16 = 752 mm < 1100 − 50 = 1050 mm available. Bearing under the column: 1800 × 10³/(300 × 500) = 12.0 N/mm² ≤ 0.45 × 20 × 2 = 18.0 N/mm².
Soil with the real weight: (1200 + 6.75 × 0.6 × 25)/6.75 = 192.8 kN/m² ≤ 200.
examples.answer: Footing 2.7 m × 2.5 m × 600 mm; 11 bars of 16 mm along the 2.7 m length and 12 bars of 16 mm along the 2.5 m width; one-way shear 0.28 ≤ 0.29 N/mm² and punching 0.79 ≤ 1.12 N/mm².

examples.question: A 400 mm square column carries a service load of 900 kN and a service moment of 90 kN·m. The safe bearing capacity is 200 kN/m². Size a rectangular footing with the moment along its length, and find the factored design moment at the column face in that direction.
steps: Service pressures (10 % self-weight): (900 + 90)/6.16 ± 90/2.875 = 160.7 ± 31.3: p<sub>max</sub> = 192.0 ≤ 200 and p<sub>min</sub> = 129.4 kN/m² > 0. (A 2.6 m length gives 209 kN/m², too high.)
Net factored pressures: 1350/6.16 ± 135/2.875: q<sub>1</sub> = 266.1 and q<sub>2</sub> = 172.2 kN/m².
At the column face on the heavy side, 1.20 m from the edge: q<sub>f</sub> = 266.1 − (266.1 − 172.2) × 1.20/2.8 = 225.9 kN/m².

Moment of the trapezoid: M<sub>u</sub> = B[q<sub>f</sub>x²/2 + (q<sub>1</sub> − q<sub>f</sub>)x²/3] = 2.2 × [225.9 × 1.20²/2 + 40.3 × 1.20²/3] = 400.3 kN·m. Using the average pressure instead would give only 347.1 kN·m.
examples.answer: 2.8 m × 2.2 m; service pressures 192 and 129 kN/m²; design moment at the heavy face 400 kN·m on the 2.2 m width.

traps: Sizing the plan with factored loads. Area uses service loads against q<sub>s</sub>; bending and shear use factored net pressure.
Taking punching at the column face, or using the column perimeter for b<sub>0</sub>. It is at d/2 from the faces.
Spreading the short-direction bars of a rectangular pad evenly. The central band of width B takes 2/(β + 1) of them.
Using the average pressure of an eccentric footing for bending. Use the trapezoid on the heavy side.
Forgetting the 150 mm minimum edge of a sloped footing, or checking its shear with the full depth at the column.

quiz.q: Write the punching shear check for a footing under an a × b column.
quiz.a: V<sub>u</sub> = P<sub>u</sub> − w<sub>u</sub>(a + d)(b + d) on b<sub>0</sub> = 2(a + b + 2d); τ<sub>v</sub> = V<sub>u</sub>/(b<sub>0</sub>d) ≤ k<sub>s</sub> 0.25√f<sub>ck</sub>, k<sub>s</sub> = 0.5 + b/a ≤ 1.

quiz.q: What is the minimum edge thickness of a footing on soil?
Why is the soil pressure for sizing taken from service loads, but the design pressure from factored loads?
quiz.a: Safe bearing capacity is a working value with its own safety factor against shear failure and settlement. The concrete and steel are designed at the limit state of collapse, so they need the factored loads.

quiz.q: Find β and the bars in the central band for a 3.6 m × 2.4 m footing with 15 short-direction bars.
quiz.a: β = 1.5; 2/(1.5 + 1) = 0.8; 0.8 × 15 = 12 bars in the central 2.4 m band and 3 in the two end strips (1 or 2 each).

quiz.q: In the second worked example, the column moment rises to 150 kN·m with the same plan. What happens?
quiz.a: e = 150/900 = 0.167 m < L/6 = 0.467 m, so no uplift, but p<sub>max</sub> = 990/6.16 + 150/2.875 = 212.9 kN/m² > 200. Lengthen the footing or offset it by e towards the moment.

quiz.q: Why does one-way shear, not bending, set the depth of most footings?
quiz.a: Footings have no stirrups, so the concrete alone must take the shear at τ<sub>c</sub>, which is low (0.3 to 0.4 N/mm² for the small steel ratios of a footing). Bending needs only about 240 mm in the first worked example, but shear needs about 530 mm.

beyond: Not for the exam. Heavy columns on poor soil need raft foundations or pile caps, and pile caps are designed by strut-and-tie models rather than beam theory. Search for "pile cap strut and tie" and "raft foundation design".
